description.narrative:
Across Cambodia, youth, women, indigenous people, and persons with disabilities continue to encounter significant barriers to participating in public financial management processes. Although the Law on Public Financial System (2018) and the National Program for Sub-National Democratic Development (NP2) provide frameworks for citizen participation, in practice these groups remain largely excluded from meaningful engagement in budgetary discussions and decision-making. This exclusion results in limited influence over the allocation of public resources and weakens downward accountability at the sub-national level. One of the main challenges is the limited awareness and knowledge of public financial management rights and processes. Many citizens, particularly those in rural or remote areas, have little understanding of the budget cycle, their rights to participate, or the formal mechanisms available to influence Commune and Sangkat Development Plans and Investment Plans. The 2023 Open Budget Survey scored Cambodia only fifteen out of one hundred on public participation, reflecting that while legal provisions exist, they are not effectively translated into practice due to inadequate outreach and civic education. This situation diminishes the ability of citizens to advocate for their needs and to demand greater accountability from sub-national administrations.
A further barrier is inequitable access to budget information. Although budget summaries are produced and published, they are often highly technical, rarely translated into indigenous languages, and inaccessible to those with limited literacy or without internet connectivity. The World Bank’s 2021 Governance Report revealed that only twenty-seven percent of rural citizens recalled seeing or hearing any budget-related information in the preceding year. For indigenous communities, language barriers and geographical remoteness further limit their opportunities to access and use budget information.Persons with disabilities also face specific obstacles when budget documents and consultations are not designed in accessible formats. Grassroots actors also face low levels of confidence and technical skill to participate effectively in budget processes. They are rarely equipped with the knowledge needed to analyze budget allocations, engage in participatory budgeting sessions, or submit proposals to official planning processes. CPDD’s civic engagement study in 2019 found that fewer than twenty percent of community-basedorganization members had ever submitted proposals for Commune Development Plans. Women and indigenous women in particular are oftenabsent from these processes, facing intersecting barriers related to both gender and ethnicity, which reduces the diversity and inclusivity of decision-making spaces.
Citizen monitoring and accountability mechanisms are also weak. While public consultation mechanisms such as commune public forums and the Commune and Sangkat Development Process exist, there is no systematic way of tracking whether the inputs collected are integrated into the final development or investment plans. Reports from the National Committee for Sub-National Democratic Development show that although seventy-four percent of communes record receiving citizen inputs during consultations, only about half of these are reflected in the final plans. The absence of transparent feedback loops erodes public trust, discourages future participation, and perpetuates the perception that citizen voices are symbolic rather than meaningful. Exclusion from national-level advocacy further deepens the problem. At the national stage, budget transparency and fiscal policy advocacy are often dominated by established civil society organizations, leaving grassroots voices underrepresented. Youth, indigenous communities,and persons with disabilities rarely have direct access to policy platforms or opportunities to engage with parliamentary committees, ministries, or national reform bodies. This perpetuates a top-down approach where local concerns do not meaningfully influence national policy reforms.
Through this project, CPDD seeks to address these challenges by equipping marginalized groups with the knowledge, skills, and confidence to engage effectively in budget processes and advocate for their priorities. The project will ensure that budget information is provided in timely, accessible, and user-friendly formats, including Khmer and indigenous languages, and informs suitable for persons with disabilities. It will strengthen citizen monitoring mechanisms that allow communities to track whether their priorities are integrated into Commune and District plans and to receive transparent feedback from authorities. It will also establish platforms for grassroots leaders to bring their perspectives into national policy reform discussions, thereby bridging the gap between local realities and national reforms.
The change that CPDD seeks to influence and advocate for is a culture of inclusive, transparent, and accountable governance in which citizens, particularly youth, women, indigenous people, and persons with disabilities, are able to participate meaningfully in budgetary processes. This change will strengthen trust between citizens and localauthorities, improve responsiveness in resource allocation, andcontribute to long-term democratic accountability.

participating-org.narrative:
The Coalition for Partnership in Democratic Development (CPDD) is a national membership-based network committed to strengthening democratic governance, decentralisation, and citizen participation in Cambodia. Our goal is to ensure that all citizens, particularly women, youth, indigenous people, and persons with disabilities, can engage meaningfully in governance processes and hold public officials accountable for transparent, inclusive, and equitable service delivery.
CPDD’s work focuses on four main areas: (1) supporting decentralization and deconcentration (D<(>&<)>D) reform through citizen and CSO engagement in sub-national governance and budget processes; (2) promoting public financial management and budget transparency via participatory budgeting, budget literacy initiatives, and policy advocacy through the Budget Working Group (BWG); (3) advancing social accountability by enabling citizen-led monitoringand fostering multi-stakeholder dialogue between communities and government; and (4) building the capacity of CSOs and grassroots networks through tailored training, mentoring, and the development of practical advocacy tools.
The achievements include coordinating joint CSO advocacy that expanded public access to budget information and formal consultation processes; leading national dialogue platforms that elevated rural and indigenous community priorities into national policy debates; producing Cambodia’s first Khmer-language budget monitoring and advocacy toolkit, now used nationwide; and establishing community monitoring groups in over 30 communes,resulting in documented citizen inputs being incorporated into Commune Development Plans and Commune Investment Plans.
What makes CPDD unique is the ability to bridge grassroots voices with national reform agendas. With a network of over 100 member organizationsand affiliates across all provinces, we combine technical policy expertise with deep community trust. This enables us to translate complex governance and budget concepts into practical, accessible tools, ensuring that even the most marginalized communities can influence the decisions that shape their futures.
